name: Hyper-IgD syndrome / mevalonate kinase deficiency spectrum

reference.source: Firestein & Kelley's Textbook of Rheumatology / EULAR recommendations for autoinflammatory diseases
clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive autoinflammatory disorder caused by mutations in MVK, encoding mevalonate kinase, that spans milder hyper-IgD syndrome to severe mevalonic aciduria
Recurrent fevers usually begin in the first year of life and last several days, often provoked by vaccination, infection or stress
Attacks characteristically feature tender cervical lymphadenopathy, abdominal pain with vomiting or diarrhoea, arthralgia, aphthous ulcers and a variable rash
A raised serum IgD, and often IgA, is supportive but neither sensitive nor specific and may be normal, especially in young children
Elevated urinary mevalonic acid during attacks reflects the underlying enzymatic block
The severe end of the spectrum (mevalonic aciduria) adds developmental delay, dysmorphism, ataxia and failure to thrive
Management targets the interleukin-1 pathway, with interleukin-1 inhibition the mainstay for frequent or severe attacks
reference.pathophysiology: Hyper-IgD syndrome lies on the mevalonate kinase deficiency spectrum, caused by biallelic MVK mutations that reduce activity of mevalonate kinase, an enzyme early in the mevalonate (isoprenoid/cholesterol) biosynthetic pathway. Reduced enzyme activity impairs production of downstream non-sterol isoprenoids, particularly geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate, which is required for prenylation of small regulatory GTPases. Deficient protein prenylation destabilises inhibitory signals on the innate immune system and enhances NLRP3 inflammasome activation with excess interleukin-1 beta release, producing recurrent inflammatory attacks. Enzyme activity worsens transiently with fever, creating a self-amplifying inflammatory cycle, and profound deficiency produces the severe multisystem phenotype of mevalonic aciduria.
additionalDifferentials: PFAPA (periodic fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, adenitis) syndrome
Recurrent infective or lymphoproliferative causes of fever with lymphadenopathy
additionalInvestigations: Serum immunoglobulins including IgD and IgA
Urinary mevalonic acid measured during a febrile attack
Acute phase reactants during and between attacks
Full blood count to document attack-related leucocytosis and exclude cyclical neutropenia
Mevalonate kinase enzyme activity assay where available
redFlags: Developmental delay, ataxia or failure to thrive suggesting the severe mevalonic aciduria phenotype
Signs of AA amyloidosis such as new proteinuria in long-standing disease
Severe dehydration from recurrent vomiting and diarrhoea during attacks
Attacks that are increasing in frequency or severity despite treatment
reference.prognosis: Attack frequency in the hyper-IgD end of the spectrum often lessens with age and responds to interleukin-1 blockade, giving a reasonable outlook, whereas severe mevalonic aciduria carries significant neurodevelopmental morbidity and higher mortality, and AA amyloidosis remains a long-term risk in poorly controlled disease.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis because serum IgD is normal, which is common in young children
Missing the diagnostic window by not collecting urine for mevalonic acid during a febrile attack
Confusing frequent early-childhood attacks with recurrent infections and treating with repeated antibiotics
Failing to recognise the more severe mevalonic aciduria phenotype in an infant with neurological features
references: EULAR recommendations for the management of autoinflammatory diseases
